strengths: MindHier offers a plausible and useful adaptation of scale-wise autoregressive generation to fMRI reconstruction, combining intermediate CLIP supervision with scale-dependent neural conditioning.
Table 1 reports competitive results across four NSD subjects and several established baselines, including strong semantic identification scores and the lowest reported SwAV distance.

The hierarchical-supervision ablation provides meaningful evidence: on Subject 1, full supervision improves PixCorr from 0.201 to 0.273 and CLIP identification from 95.4% to 97.2% over final-layer supervision.
The appendix includes per-subject results, limited-data experiments, optimization details, and qualitative examples that supplement the main evaluation.
weaknesses: The central contribution is insufficiently isolated. The proposed system changes the pretrained generator, supervision, and conditioning simultaneously. Missing controls include giving every generation scale access to all hierarchical features and applying comparable hierarchical guidance to diffusion. The inverted-routing comparison alone does not establish that the proposed correspondence is necessary or uniquely suited to autoregression.

The inference and comparison protocols are underspecified. Appendix E selects among four candidates using CLIP similarity but does not identify the reference used for selection, making it impossible to verify that selection uses only information available at inference. Hardware, batching, baseline sampling settings, and whether candidate generation and selection are included in timing are also unspecified, weakening the claimed 4.67× speedup.

The determinism argument is technically unsupported: conditioning the initial token on fMRI does not eliminate randomness in subsequent autoregressive sampling. Four visibly different teddy-bear reconstructions and the best-of-four inference protocol do not establish deterministic behavior. Dataset-wide variability measurements and matched sampling controls are needed.

Structural-fidelity claims exceed the evidence. Without auxiliary low-level features, MindHier trails MindEye2 substantially in PixCorr (0.235 versus 0.322) and SSIM (0.381 versus 0.431). The auxiliary variant improves these metrics, but its integration is not adequately described and its semantic scores decline. Qualitative grounding examples lack quantitative localization results or baseline comparisons.

Important implementation details remain missing or inconsistent: voxel tokenization and encoder dimensions, caption sourcing, feature pooling/projections, sampling settings, and auxiliary-feature integration. Equation 2 is a hard-target contrastive loss rather than a soft-target SoftCLIP objective; Algorithm 1 also uses the terminal feature inside the intermediate-layer MSE loop. These ambiguities hinder reproduction.

Statistical support is limited. Table 1 does not explain its uncertainty estimates or number of runs, while all principal ablations use only Subject 1 without uncertainty. The one-session experiment specifies limited data for generator fine-tuning but does not clearly establish that encoder training follows the same restriction.

The neuroscience and positioning claims are overstated. Regressing voxel responses from features already computed from fMRI requires carefully held-out evaluation and controls to substantiate biological hierarchy, which are not reported. Likewise, characterizing diffusion methods as uniformly collapsing neural information into one vector overlooks the auxiliary low-level pathways acknowledged in Table 1.

strengths: MindHier offers a coherent adaptation of scale-wise image generation to fMRI reconstruction, combining intermediate CLIP supervision with scale-dependent neural conditioning.
Table 1 reports promising semantic reconstruction results across four NSD subjects, including 96.4% CLIP identification accuracy and 0.329 SwAV distance.
The controlled comparisons in Tables 2–3 provide useful evidence for intermediate supervision and examine the tradeoff between semantic and low-level fidelity.
The appendix includes per-subject results, additional qualitative examples, and training hyperparameters.
weaknesses: The central mechanism is insufficiently isolated. Table 4 compares the proposed routing only against reversed routing; it lacks an equally supervised baseline that exposes all hierarchical features at every scale. Consequently, the gains cannot be cleanly attributed to the prescribed coarse-to-fine correspondence rather than richer conditioning and supervision. No matched hierarchical-conditioning diffusion baseline tests the claimed need to move beyond diffusion.

Evaluation details leave important fairness questions unresolved. Appendix E selects the best of four reconstructions using CLIP similarity without specifying the reference used for selection or whether all baselines receive the same candidate budget. The manuscript also does not establish how every baseline was evaluated on the updated 1,000-image test set. These ambiguities materially affect confidence in the comparisons.

The deterministic-generation claim is unsupported. Autoregressive token generation can remain stochastic despite a deterministic starting embedding, and the sampling policy is unspecified. Four visually similar reconstructions of one teddy bear, compared only with MindBridge, do not establish dataset-wide stability or superiority to controlled diffusion sampling.

The efficiency comparison lacks hardware, precision, batch size, diffusion sampling settings, and clarification of whether candidate generation, selection, and auxiliary processing are included. Moreover, the reported MindEye2 times imply 12.14/2.64 ≈ 4.60×, rather than 4.67×. The evidence does not substantiate the stronger claim of fundamental computational superiority.

Structural-fidelity claims exceed the evidence. Without auxiliary features, MindHier trails MindEye2 substantially in PixCorr (0.235 versus 0.322) and SSIM (0.381 versus 0.431). The auxiliary variant improves these metrics, but its integration is not explained sufficiently to reproduce or attribute the gains. Brain grounding is illustrated through selected examples without quantitative localization results or baseline comparisons.

Reproducibility remains incomplete: voxel tokenization, encoder dimensions, sampling settings, and the auxiliary low-level pathway are insufficiently specified. Equation 2 describes a hard-target contrastive objective despite being called SoftCLIP, and Algorithm 1 inconsistently uses the terminal feature inside the intermediate-alignment loop. The one-session experiment also leaves unclear whether the encoder itself was trained using only that session.

The neuroscience interpretation is stronger than the analysis supports. Regressing voxel responses from features already derived from fMRI requires explicit held-out evaluation and quantitative regional comparisons; Appendix D supplies qualitative maps without these controls. This does not establish cognitive alignment or disentanglement.

Statistical support is limited: the meaning and replication count of the reported ± values are unspecified, baseline uncertainty is absent, and ablations use only Subject 1. Several headline improvements are modest, so their reliability remains unclear.

strengths: The combination of hierarchical fMRI-to-CLIP alignment and scale-dependent conditioning of a pretrained visual autoregressive generator is coherent and relevant to brain-image reconstruction.

Table 1 reports competitive results across four NSD subjects, including strong semantic metrics: 96.4% CLIP identification and 0.329 SwAV distance. Improvements on multiple feature extractors provide evidence beyond the CLIP training objective.

The hierarchical-supervision ablation provides concrete positive evidence: on Subject 1, full supervision improves PixCorr from 0.201 to 0.273 and CLIP identification from 95.4% to 97.2% over final-layer-only supervision. Layer-selection and reversed-guidance experiments further investigate the design.
weaknesses: The evaluation protocol leaves consequential ambiguities. Appendix E selects the best of four reconstructions using CLIP similarity without specifying the reference embedding. It must establish that selection uses only information available from fMRI at inference, and that baselines receive equivalent candidate budgets. The provenance and reevaluation procedure for baseline scores on the updated 1,000-image test set are also insufficiently documented.

The principal ablations do not isolate the necessity of scale-specific routing. A matched baseline exposing all hierarchically supervised features at every scale is missing; reversing their order does not establish superiority over unrestricted conditioning. Ablations cover only Subject 1, and Table 1's uncertainty estimates lack a definition and number of runs.

The claimed deterministic nature is unsupported. Conditioning an autoregressive model on fMRI does not eliminate randomness in token sampling; Appendix E explicitly generates multiple candidates, and Figure 4 shows varying outputs. One stimulus across four trials is insufficient to establish lower variability, robustness, or faithful repeatability across the dataset.

The headline efficiency claim is not reproducible without hardware, precision, batching, baseline sampling settings, and clarification of whether timing includes four-candidate generation, ranking, and auxiliary processing. Moreover, the tabulated MindEye2 runtime implies approximately 4.60× acceleration, rather than 4.67×.

Important implementation details remain unclear, including fMRI tokenization and encoder dimensions, sampling settings, and incorporation of the auxiliary low-level feature responsible for the strongest structural metrics. Equation 2 is a hard-positive contrastive objective despite being called SoftCLIP. The pseudocode also contains inconsistent layer indexing and uses e_M where the intermediate e_m is intended.

The motivation overgeneralizes prior diffusion methods as collapsing neural information into a single high-level vector, despite existing structural and multilevel conditioning approaches, including cited work. A more precise comparison with these methods is needed to establish novelty beyond adapting Switti with intermediate-feature supervision.

Several conclusions exceed the evidence. Without auxiliary features, structural metrics are not consistently best. The one-session experiment does not clarify whether the fMRI encoder also sees only one session. Brain grounding is qualitative and receives ground-truth object labels, while the neuroscience analysis lacks quantitative held-out validation and controls. These results do not establish the broad claims of structural superiority, data efficiency, and cognitive alignment.
